fact_claims.verbatim: Halcyon’s relevant figures: flagship 55 °C sustained-heat test failure rate is 3.9%
company-wide thermal incidents last year were 8.1 per 100,000 installed units
and the flagship rate was 9.9 per 100,000
81% of installed units support remote emergency shut-off
Northwind’s figures: company-wide thermal incidents were 8.6 per 100,000 installed units last year
38% of installed units support remote shut-off
One additional S1-relevant Northwind figure: 3 thermal incidents last year were not reported to any regulator.
For S1 evidence, Halcyon had 4 thermal incidents last year that were not reported to any regulator.

S1_incident_reporting.quote: Manufacturers must report to the relevant regulator any thermal event involving fire, smoke, uncontrolled overheating, injury, property damage, emergency-service response, or a safety-related shutdown within 24 hours of learning of it, with a written preliminary report within 5 business days. Any other suspected thermal incident must be reported within 10 business days. Customers whose unit is involved must be notified directly within 5 business days, or sooner where an immediate hazard warrants it.

S2_thermal_testing.quote: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol and representative production units. Manufacturers must submit per-model results, sample size, protocol, and corrective-action records to the regulator and provide the per-model test results directly to customers who buy or are considering buying that model. Results need not be published for the general public. A model exceeding a 5% failure rate must be promptly reported to the regulator and affected customers, investigated, and subject to a corrective-action plan and retesting. Exceeding 5% alone does not require a sales ban; the regulator may restrict sales if the manufacturer fails to provide or implement an adequate plan, or if the regulator finds an unreasonable safety risk.

S3_remote_shutoff.quote: New units must support secure remote emergency shut-off, with safeguards against unauthorized access and a local means of operation. Manufacturers must provide a retrofit pathway for installed units that lack this capability and complete retrofits within 6 years of this standard taking effect. Where retrofitting is technically infeasible, the manufacturer must notify affected customers and the regulator, explain the limitation, and provide an equivalent risk-reduction measure.

S4_fire_suppression.quote: New units must include built-in fire suppression no later than 36 months after this standard is adopted. Suppression systems must be appropriate to the battery chemistry and installation, and designed and tested to limit fire spread and protect occupants and nearby persons.

S5_customer_disclosure.quote: A recall is mandatory when any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year. Manufacturers must promptly notify the regulator and affected customers, explain the risk and remedy, and provide safe shutdown or other interim instructions where needed. A recall is also required when the regulator determines that a serious defect creates an unreasonable risk, regardless of the incident-rate threshold; a recall requires an effective safety remedy and does not by itself mandate a permanent sales ban.

document.section_notes: The final rules mandate strong incident reporting and customer notice, require 55°C testing with a 5% limit and direct customer results but no public publication or automatic sales ban, and set a 6-year retrofit deadline. S4 requires built-in suppression at 36 months. S5 mandates recall at 8/100k with prompt notices and a serious-risk clause, which strongly favours Northwind because its Hearth 10 is below the trigger while Halcyon's Ember 8 is above it.
